summary: Defines a registration mechanism for the Host Identity Protocol so hosts can sign up with services such as rendezvous servers or middleboxes. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 8003.

eli5.summary: Before a friend can find you through a message desk, you register with the desk. This describes how HIP hosts register.

questions: how to register with a hip rendezvous server
subtitle: Hosts can register with services in HIP by exchanging registration parameters.

tldr.problem: HIP systems needed a way for hosts to register with services such as rendezvous servers or middleboxes, but the base HIP specification did not define this mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds four new message parameters (REG_INFO, REG_REQUEST, REG_RESPONSE, and REG_FAILED) that allow a requester host to ask for services and a registrar to grant or deny them during a HIP session.
tldr.outcome: HIP hosts can now sign up for services with time-limited registrations that can be refreshed or cancelled. This was superseded by RFC 8003.

today: RFC 5203 is an experimental RFC that was superseded by RFC 8003. The later specification provides an updated approach to HIP registration.

sections.title: HIP Registration Mechanism
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) is a framework for network communication that uses host identifiers separate from IP addresses. This extension defines how HIP hosts can register with services such as rendezvous servers (which help hosts find each other) or middleboxes (devices that help with network traversal). The registration mechanism allows a requester host to ask a registrar host to provide a service, and the registrar to grant access to the service for a limited time.

This document does not define how requesters discover registrars, only how they register once they have found one. It uses the HIP base exchange to establish a secure association and adds new parameters to negotiate registration within that association.
sections.eli5: HIP is a system where each computer has an identity. Some computers offer services (like a meeting place), and others want to use them. This says how to sign up.

sections.title: How Registration Works
sections.content:
Registration happens in several steps. First, a registrar announces the services it offers by including a REG_INFO parameter in its R1 messages during the HIP base exchange. The requester sees this and can ask to register by including a REG_REQUEST parameter in either its I2 (initial contact) or UPDATE message. The registrar then evaluates the request and replies with a REG_RESPONSE parameter containing the services it granted, and optionally REG_FAILED parameters for services it denied.

Each registration has a finite lifetime, ranging from 4 milliseconds to 178 days. Both the requester and registrar can cancel a registration at any time. The registrar announces new services or removes them by sending UPDATE messages with fresh REG_INFO parameters. A requester can refresh an existing registration by sending another REG_REQUEST before the current one expires.
sections.eli5: The registrar says what services it has. The requester asks for the ones it wants. The registrar says which ones it will provide, and for how long. When the time is up, either can say they are done.

sections.title: Registration Message Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC defines four new HIP parameters. REG_INFO (type 930) is sent by a registrar to announce what it offers, including the minimum and maximum registration lifetime in exponentially encoded 8-bit fields and a list of service types. REG_REQUEST (type 932) is sent by a requester and lists the service types it wants and how long it wants them for. REG_RESPONSE (type 934) confirms the services the registrar granted and their lifetime. REG_FAILED (type 936) lists services that could not be granted and why (for example, missing credentials or service unavailable).

Registrars set a minimum lifetime (at least 10 seconds) and maximum (at least 120 seconds) to define reasonable bounds for service registration. A zero lifetime in a request means the requester is canceling that registration. The parameters are protected by HIP signatures so they cannot be forged.
sections.eli5: These are just message fields that say what services are offered, what is requested, what was approved, and what failed. They protect registrations with encryption so nobody cheats.

sections.title: Maintaining Registrations
sections.content:
When a registrar receives a REG_REQUEST, it authenticates the requester using the host identity from the HIP association, then checks whether that host is authorized to register for the requested services based on its local policies. Authorization details are not specified here; they depend on the service type and the registrar's rules. After authorization, a REG_RESPONSE is sent with the granted services and their lifetimes, and optionally REG_FAILED for any denials.

If a registrar needs more credentials to decide, it sends back a REG_FAILED parameter with failure type 0 (needs more credentials). The requester can then try again with additional credentials after the HIP association is established. A requester must be ready to receive any lifetime value from the registrar, even outside the minimum and maximum it announced, and must not assume the granted lifetime matches the requested one.
sections.eli5: The registrar checks that a requester is who it says it is, then looks at its rules to decide. Sometimes it says yes, sometimes no, sometimes it needs more proof. The registration stays active until it expires or somebody cancels it.

sections.title: Security and Threat Model
sections.content:
This extension relies on the HIP base exchange for security and does not modify it. The HIP base exchange already provides digital signatures and HMAC for authentication and integrity. The only new threat is the creation of soft registration state at the registrar: a registrar stores information about which hosts are registered for which services.

Registrars are assumed to act on a voluntary basis and are willing to store HIP association state for previously unknown hosts. Since they already store HIP associations, storing time-limited registration state does not introduce serious additional threats. A registrar can cancel registrations at any time, even before expiry, which helps during attacks or when resources are constrained.
sections.eli5: Registrations do not add new security risks because HIP already protects everything. The registrar can always say no or cancel if something looks wrong.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Extensibility
sections.content:
The RFC assigns four new HIP parameter type values: REG_INFO (930), REG_REQUEST (932), REG_RESPONSE (934), and REG_FAILED (936). It also allocates a notify message code 51 for REG_REQUIRED errors. These allow applications to define specific service types by assigning values in the registration type namespace.

The RFC opens two new IANA registries: one for registration types (for service identifiers) and one for failure types (reasons why registration failed). Values 0-200 in each are unassigned and can be allocated through new IETF specifications, while 201-255 are reserved for private experimental use.
sections.eli5: This registers some official numbers that other protocols can build on to define specific services and error reasons.
